# Today: the high-speed train and the ordinary flight

Today London is two and a quarter hours from Paris by train, closer in time than Lille was in 1850. Almost every city on Earth lies within a day. Yet for the longest journeys, the clock has barely moved since the 1970s: what has changed is not speed but price, frequency and the sheer number of people travelling.

### A traveller: the first Eurostar passengers, 1994

On Monday 14 November 1994, the first fare-paying passengers travelled through the Channel Tunnel from London to Paris and Brussels, reaching both capitals in about three hours [@first-passengers-go]. The train pulled into the Gare du Nord a few minutes early; most of the passengers had booked their seats years in advance [@first-passengers-go], which is patience of a very British kind. A standard-class ticket cost £95 booked two weeks ahead (about $330 today) or £155 for a flexible fare (about $530) [@first-passengers-go; @100-1990-2026; @gbp-usd-historical].

The 50 km tunnel had taken six years and £10 billion to build [@first-passengers-go]. In 1994 the 790-seat trains reached 288 km/h in France but were held to 160 km/h on the old tracks of south-east England [@first-passengers-go], where the high-speed line took rather longer to arrive than the trains. Once a dedicated high-speed line to London was completed, the journey from St Pancras to the Gare du Nord fell to 2 hours 15 minutes [@high-speed-1]. A journey that took four or five days around 1800, and seven and a half hours by the boat trains of the 1890s, now takes about as long as a feature film.

### The maps

![Europe from Paris today](/maps/output/europe_today.png){#fig-europe-today fig-alt="Europe from Paris today: isochrone map of fastest travel times"}

France and its neighbours now fall almost entirely within six hours, much of it within three by high-speed train. The slowest parts of the European map are no longer the far edges of the continent, but places cut off by borders and politics: Moscow, a single flight of about five and a half hours in 1975, has had no direct flights from France since March 2022 and now takes 10 to 13 hours door to door via a connection [@aller-russie-depuis].

![The world from Paris today](/maps/output/world_today.png){#fig-world-today fig-alt="The world from Paris today: isochrone map of fastest travel times"}

The world map is almost uniformly warm. New York lies about ten hours away, Tokyo and Hong Kong about fifteen or sixteen, Sydney about a day. Compared with 1975, the colours have barely shifted: long-haul jets fly at much the same speed as fifty years ago.

### Travel times from Paris today

| Destination | Fastest journey | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lille | about 1 hour | Estimate, by TGV |
| Brussels | about 1½ hours | Estimate, by high-speed train |
| Lyon | about 2 hours | Estimate, by TGV |
| London | 2 hours 15 minutes | Eurostar timetable [@high-speed-1] |
| Rome, Madrid, Berlin | about 4 hours | Estimates, by air including airport time |
| Cairo | about 6 hours | Estimate |
| New York | about 10 hours | Estimate, by air including airport time |
| Bombay (Mumbai) | about 11½ hours | Estimate |
| Moscow | about 12 hours | No direct flights since 2022; 10–13 hours door to door via a connection [@aller-russie-depuis] |
| Tokyo | about 16 hours | Estimate |
| Sydney | about 24 hours | Estimate, with one connection |

### Conditions on the road

The experience of speed has split in two. Within Europe, the high-speed train runs from city centre to city centre. Between continents, travel is by jet at speeds little changed since the 1970s; supersonic travel ended with Concorde's retirement in 2003 [@air-france-commemorates].

### Paying the way

For most journeys from Paris, paying has become almost invisible: a card or a phone works nearly everywhere, and within the euro area there is no currency to exchange at all. Moscow is again the exception. Since March 2022, when Visa and Mastercard suspended their operations in Russia, cards issued abroad no longer work there [@visa-mastercard-suspend], so a traveller from Paris must carry cash, much as travellers did before the circular note.

### Risks

Travel has never been safer. Airline travel is now the safest form of transport: more people die in car accidents in the United States in three months than have died in the entire history of commercial flight [@evolution-commercial-flying]. The rare crashes, such as the Concorde accident of 25 July 2000, are remembered precisely because they are so rare [@evolution-commercial-flying; @air-france-commemorates].

### Who travels, and how many

Numbers have exploded. In 2025 nearly five billion travellers took to the skies, on nearly 40 million flights [@annual-review]. Paris's two main airports alone handled more than 100 million passengers in 2025: about 72 million at Charles de Gaulle and 35 million at Orly [@december-full-year; @orly-airport]. Where about 140 vehicles a day passed on the new roads outside Paris in 1788, and a few dozen passengers braved a winter Atlantic crossing in 1850, travel is now a routine part of ordinary lives. Crossing the road calls for rather more care than it did.
